title: Deceit requires a false representation made knowingly, without belief in its truth or recklessly, intended to induce reliance and causing damage

content.overview: Deceit requires a false representation made knowingly, without belief in its truth or recklessly, intended to induce reliance and causing damage. Negligent misstatement is distinct and depends on a duty of care in making the statement.
content.glance: Deceit requires a false representation made knowingly, without belief in its truth or recklessly, intended to induce reliance and causing damage. Negligent misstatement is distinct and depends on a duty of care in making the statement.
content.study: Deceit requires a false representation made knowingly, without belief in its truth or recklessly, intended to induce reliance and causing damage. Negligent misstatement is distinct and depends on a duty of care in making the statement.\n\nDerry v Peek sets the classic deceit standard. Hedley Byrne recognised negligent misstatement in appropriate relationships involving assumption of responsibility.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: Derry v Peek sets the classic deceit standard. Hedley Byrne recognised negligent misstatement in appropriate relationships involving assumption of responsibility.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: These torts are common-law and overlap with contract and consumer remedies. Silence is not generally deceit unless circumstances create a duty to disclose or make a representation misleading.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: Deceit: false representation, fraudulent state of mind, intent to induce, reliance and damage. Negligent misstatement: duty, breach, reasonable reliance, causation and loss.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: Emails, statements, documents, expert reports and transaction records may prove representation and reliance.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: Plead the exact representation and reliance. Identify whether the claim is deceit, negligent misstatement, contract or consumer deficiency. Limitation depends on the cause.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Deceit requires fraudulent knowledge or recklessness; negligent misstatement turns on duty, reasonable reliance and breach.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Fraudulent state of mind and causative reliance are essential to deceit.

distinctions.right: Deceit requires fraud; negligent misstatement may arise from careless advice where a duty exists.
